chapter_theme: The last kaathai (வரந்தரு காதை) closes the story by showing deeds and loves of the past bearing fruit in the present: Devanthi tells the Chera of Manimekalai's renunciation, is possessed by the god Saathan, and through water from a spring that restores former births three girls in Vanchi are shown to be Kannaki's mother, Kovalan's mother and Maadari reborn near the pathini; Maadalan explains it as the old law of births and deeds, the king endows the pathini's temple, foreign kings beg her presence and a voice grants the boon, the goddess tells the poet's own renunciation, and the poet ends with a string of commands to his hearers.

cast.role: the Chera king of Vanchi who brought the stone from the north and set up the pathini's temple; called here வானவர் பெருந்தகை, குறிஞ்சிக் கோமான், மன்னர் கோ
Kannaki's friend, the Brahmin woman whose husband was the god Saathan; here possessed by him
the god Saathan of the sects, who once took the form of Maalathi's dead child and became Devanthi's husband; here he speaks through her
Brahmin of Thalaichengaanam who knows Kovalan's past deeds and explains the rebirths to the king
a Brahmin's wife whose co-wife's baby choked on the milk she gave it
the dancer-courtesan of Puhar with whom Kovalan lived, mother of Manimekalai
Madhavi's mother, who asks Madhavi what is to be done with the grown Manimekalai
the daughter of Madhavi and Kovalan, given to the Buddhist dharma as a girl (not the sea goddess of the same name)
Kama, the bodiless god of love
the unnamed Chola king of Puhar
the ascetics of true speech of Puhar to whom Manimekalai announces her renunciation

the three little girls of Vanchi, the twin daughters of Arattan Chetti and the young daughter of Sedakkudumbi, who on being sprinkled recall former births as Kannaki's mother, Kovalan's mother and Maadari
the aged herdswoman (ஆயர் முதுமகள்) of Madurai in whose house Kannaki lodged, reborn as Sedakkudumbi's daughter
merchant of Puhar, Kannaki's husband, killed in Madurai
Kovalan's wife, the pathini, now a goddess (இமையோர் இளங்கொடி)
the visiting kings before the Chera: the Aryan kings freed from prison, the kings released from the great prison, the Kongar of Kudagam and the Malava kings
Gajabahu, king of sea-girt Lanka, among the kings who beg the goddess's presence
the Chera prince who gave up kingship; the poet, who here speaks in the first person
the hearers of the poem, whom the poet addresses at its close

silappathikaram:30:1-23.reading: After the goddess's form has passed from his sight, the Chera king turns to Devanthi and asks who the Manimekalai is for whom she cried out and why she renounced; Devanthi, wishing his rule and land prosperity, begins: the girl had come to full youth, her eyes knew love's craft though she herself did not, her body had ripened in every part, the dance master stood ready behind her, and Madhavi's mother asked Madhavi what she intended and what she should do.
silappathikaram:30:1-23.nuance: The catalogue of the girl's ripened body (lines 10 to 19) is the courtesan house's reckoning of a daughter ready for the stage, with the dance master already waiting (line 20); the renunciation that follows is set against exactly this readiness. Line 21, that the chief men of the clan would not take her by their custom, can be read as the courtesan house's worry or as the families' refusal of a courtesan's daughter in marriage; the reading leaves it open. Line 13 makes a small irony: the eyes knew the craft of love, she did not.
silappathikaram:30:1-23.event: Senguttuvan asks Devanthi why Manimekalai renounced, and Devanthi begins by telling how Madhavi's mother, seeing the girl grown, asked Madhavi what to do with her.
silappathikaram:30:1-23.unit_note: End moved from line 22 to line 23: the mother's question at lines 22 and 23 is one clause, and line 23 names who asks it.

silappathikaram:30:24-34.reading: Madhavi called her young daughter Manimekalai and, while Kama flung his great bow and fragrant arrows on the bare ground, removed the garland together with the girl's hair and gave her at the Bodhi seat into the dharma; the king and the city, hearing it, grieved like men who have dropped a fine gem into the sea, and the ascetics of true speech said with love and grace that the girl had declared her renunciation to them.
silappathikaram:30:24-34.nuance: Who removes the hair is not named: the sentence runs on from Madhavi's call, and the next unit says the girl herself left off her adornment. போதித் தானம் (line 28) can be the gift made at the Bodhi or the Bodhi as a place; either way the giving is the scene of Kovalan's dream (15:101-104), where Madhavi gives Manimekalai before the dharma-one of the Bodhi and Kama casts his arrows on the bare ground, here told as done. The grief of king and city (lines 29 to 31) treats a girl's renunciation as a public loss, the loss of the gem of the town's arts.
silappathikaram:30:24-34.event: Madhavi gives Manimekalai to the Buddhist dharma, her hair and garland removed, and Puhar's king and people grieve while the ascetics receive her.
silappathikaram:30:24-34.unit_note: Start moved from line 23 to line 24 and end from line 33 to line 34: line 33 ends in என்றே, and the sentence closes with கூறினர் at line 34.

silappathikaram:30:35-52.reading: Devanthi tells the king she wailed because the girl left off her adornment before her time; then her hair falls loose, her brows quiver, she bites her lip, her words blur, her face sweats, her eyes redden, she flings her arms and rises, and possessed by a god she speaks before the hill-country king: among the women come to see the goddess's consecration are the twin daughters of Arattan Chetti's wife and the young daughter of Sedakkudumbi, servant of the god who lies on the serpent.
silappathikaram:30:35-52.nuance: The signs of possession are listed one per half-line (lines 38 to 44) in the same piled style as the girl's body in the first unit, so the kaathai sets a body made ready for desire beside a body taken by a god. The voice is not Devanthi's own: the god names himself only at line 69. The three girls are introduced by their present parents before anything is said of who they were.
silappathikaram:30:35-52.event: Devanthi explains her cry, falls into possession and, before Senguttuvan, points out three girls among the women at the consecration.
silappathikaram:30:35-52.unit_note: Start moved from line 34 to line 35 and end from line 50 to line 52: the sentence naming the three girls closes with ஈங்குளள் at line 52.

silappathikaram:30:53-64.reading: The possessing voice says that on the high hill by the shrine of the Lady of Good Fortune, among the pools filling the ridge, there is a spring of grinding stones and splashing water in which those who bathe become again the persons of their former birth, and that it brought that water and gave it, in a pot hanging in a sling, into the hand of the one sitting in the assembly at the lady's shrine as a token.
silappathikaram:30:53-64.nuance: The spring does not purify or grant a wish, the usual work of a holy tank; it makes a past birth come back into the present body. The one addressed (இருந்தோய், line 62) is Maadalan, as line 70 shows.
silappathikaram:30:53-64.event: Speaking through Devanthi, the god tells of a spring on the hill that restores former births and says he once gave its water to Maadalan in a pot.
silappathikaram:30:53-64.unit_note: Start moved from line 51 to line 53: the sentence about the three girls ends at line 52.

silappathikaram:30:65-91.reading: The voice says the water keeps its divine power till sunset and bids Maadalan sprinkle the three girls so that their hidden births appear, naming itself Paasandan come upon the Brahmin woman; the king is amazed, and Maadalan tells him the story: Maalathi's co-wife's baby, fed at her breast, died when an old deed flared up, she lay in vigil at Paasandan's shrine, the god came in the child's form, grew up in the old Brahmin family, married Devanthi, and after eight years showed his ageless youth, told her to come to his shrine and left; later, appearing as a Brahmin at the shrine of the Lady of Good Fortune, he gave Maadalan the pot and a token and went away for good.
silappathikaram:30:65-91.nuance: Maadalan's telling repeats the Maalathi story of the dream kaathai (9:1-44) with a change: there Maalathi carried the child round the city's shrines, here she lies in vigil at Paasandan's own shrine, and the child's death is put down to பழவினை (line 75), an old deed flaring up, which the earlier telling does not say. The god's parting words to Devanthi, எம் கோட்டத்து நீ வா, are given here as என் கோட்டத்து நீவா (lines 86 to 87), and the chapter shows how they are kept: he comes back to her not as a husband but as the god who possesses her.
silappathikaram:30:65-91.event: The god tells Maadalan to sprinkle the water on the three girls, and Maadalan tells the amazed king how Saathan came as Maalathi's dead child, married Devanthi and later gave him the pot.

claims.claim: a deed of a former time flares up and brings death even on an infant

silappathikaram:30:65-91.unit_note: End moved from line 80 to line 91, absorbing the former unit 81-96 up to line 91: line 80 ends in a quotation still running into line 81, and the account of Saathan closes with போயினன் வாரான் at line 91.

silappathikaram:30:92-111.reading: Maadalan says that because he brought the water, the knowing god has now appeared on this Brahmin woman and told him to sprinkle it, and he sprinkles the girls; their hidden births return and they cry out: one as a mother to the daughter she bore, who suffered alone with her husband in a strange land, one as a mother whose heart cannot bear that her son went off into the dark with the girl who lived with her, and one who came back from the Vaigai's ford, heard the news, found the house empty and asks the young one where she has hidden.
silappathikaram:30:92-111.nuance: The girls do not say who they were: the three griefs (for a daughter, for a son and for a girl who had lodged in the house) identify Kannaki's mother, Kovalan's mother and Maadari, and Maadalan names them only in the next units. Lines 102 and 103 run several forms of address together (daughter, companion, lady who ends grief), and how the lines divide among the three voices is not certain. The scene is offered as proof of former birth seen by a whole court.
silappathikaram:30:92-111.event: Maadalan sprinkles the water on the three girls, and they cry out in the voices of the mothers of Kannaki and Kovalan and of Maadari.
silappathikaram:30:92-111.unit_note: Start moved from line 97 to line 92 and the former units 81-96 and 97-111 regrouped: the sprinkling (line 96) and its result (line 97) are one sentence, so the account of the pot from line 92 joins the laments.

silappathikaram:30:112-131.reading: When the lisping little girls have wept in the courtyard with the words of old women before the king, he looks at Maadalan, who blesses him and explains: because the mothers loved the wife of the man who entered the elephant's trunk to end a Brahmin's distress and so won the form of the gods, and had not done the unfailing dharma that goes with those of the upper world, they came as twins to Arattan Chetti's wife in old Vanchi, near the woman of the golden creeper whom they loved.
silappathikaram:30:112-131.nuance: Two fruits of deeds are set side by side: Kovalan's rescue of the Brahmin from the elephant (15:42-53) has earned him a god's form, while the mothers' love, without the dharma that leads upward, has earned them a new birth near the beloved. Love here is not condemned; it decides where they are born. The phrase கையகம் புக்கு (line 121) repeats the wording of the rescue scene (15:49).
silappathikaram:30:112-131.event: Maadalan tells the king that Kannaki's and Kovalan's mothers, bound by love for Kannaki, were reborn as Arattan Chetti's twins in Vanchi.

claims.claim: saving another from death at the risk of one's own life wins the form of the gods
those who love a person but have not done the dharma that leads upward are reborn near the one they love rather than going to the upper world

silappathikaram:30:112-131.unit_note: End moved from line 126 to line 131: line 126 is mid-sentence, and the account of the twins closes with தோன்றினர் at line 131.

silappathikaram:30:132-146.reading: Maadalan goes on that the old herdswoman, out of love for the girl from her former birth, has become Sedakkudumbi's young daughter; that the good reach the golden world, those of loving heart go where their attachment leads, the fruits of virtue and of wrong ripen, the born die and the dead are born, and none of this is new but the ancient way of life; and that the king, born by the grace of the one who rides the bull, has seen the fruit of austerity and the forms of the great as if in his hand, and should live and guard the world age after age.
silappathikaram:30:132-146.nuance: Lines 136 to 140 are the kaathai's general law, and they finish what the patikam set out (0:55-57): there the deed of the past comes in wrath to be eaten; here good deeds ripen as surely as wrong ones, and love is a force like deed that carries a person to a new birth. The Brahmin calls the Chera born of Siva's grace (line 141); this is his praise of the king, not a claim the poem makes about the pathini cult.
silappathikaram:30:132-146.event: Maadalan says Maadari was reborn as Sedakkudumbi's daughter, states the law of births and deeds, and blesses the king.

claims.claim: those who did good reach the golden world, and those whose hearts are full of love go where their attachment leads
the fruits of virtue and of wrongdoing both ripen
the born die and the dead are born, and this is the ancient order of life, nothing new
the king was born by the grace of Siva, the rider of the bull

silappathikaram:30:132-146.unit_note: Start moved from line 127 to line 132 and end from line 144 to line 146: Maadalan's speech closes with the blessing ending என்ற at line 146.

silappathikaram:30:147-164.reading: Glad with Maadalan, the king endows the temple of the pathini of unaging body who twisted off her breast so that fierce fire spread through Koodal of the Pandya land, orders a festival there every day, gives Devanthi charge of its flowers, incense and scents, and goes round it three times and bows; before him the Aryan kings freed from prison, the kings released from the great prison, the Kongar of Kudagam, the Malava kings and Gajabahu of sea-girt Lanka pray her to come to the festival they will hold in their lands as on this day of the Chera's sacrifice, and a voice rises: I have granted the boon.
silappathikaram:30:147-164.nuance: The kaathai's name comes from line 164, and the boon is asked by foreign and conquered kings, some just let out of the Chera's prison: the cult of the Madurai pathini spreads through the very kings defeated in the campaign for her stone. The temple is identified by the burning of Madurai, not by Kannaki's name. The epithet இமய வரம்பன் (line 161) is given here to the Chera holding the sacrifice; in the Patitruppattu's second decade the name belongs to Senguttuvan's father, so the two uses should not be merged. Line 162's construction (whose festival, held where) is compressed and the reading follows the plainest sense.
silappathikaram:30:147-164.event: Senguttuvan endows the pathini's temple with daily worship under Devanthi, the visiting kings beg the goddess to come to their lands, and a voice grants the boon.
silappathikaram:30:147-164.unit_note: Start moved from line 145 to line 147 and end from line 160 to line 164: the kings' prayer runs from line 157 to line 163 and is answered at line 164.

silappathikaram:30:165-185.reading: When the king, the kings and the army have praised in turn and the king has left the sacrificial hall with Maadalan, who longs for the true path like those who have seen release, the poet says that he too went, and the young creeper of the gods, shining on Devanthi, rose before him and told his own story: that when he sat in his father's shade in the jewelled hall of Vanchi and a man said he bore the mark of one who will sit as king, he looked at the man in anger and, to end Senguttuvan's distress, put away the burden of the wide earth and became, far beyond where thought can reach, a king ruling endless bliss; and he calls the hearers good people who have heard clearly these words that told her story.
silappathikaram:30:165-185.nuance: Only here does the narrator say 'I' (யானுஞ் சென்றேன், line 171), and the poem's frame closes in a circle: the goddess whose story the poet told tells the poet's own story, and the poem is named in line 184 as the words that told hers. The patikam (0:1-2) only says that Ilango gave up the throne; this unit gives the cause, a prophecy of kingship that would have set brother against brother, and makes the renunciation an act of care for Senguttuvan. பகல்செல் வாயில் (line 179), the gate of the day's going, places where he lives; the patikam names the eastern-gate shrine, and the unit's phrase is left as written.
silappathikaram:30:165-185.event: The poet follows the king out of the sacrificial hall, and the goddess, appearing on Devanthi, tells how he renounced the throne on hearing a prophecy that he would be king.

claims.claim: one who gives up the burden of a kingdom becomes king of an endless bliss beyond the reach of thought

silappathikaram:30:165-185.unit_note: Start moved from line 161 to line 165: the kings' prayer and the boon close at line 164.

silappathikaram:30:186-202.reading: The poet bids his hearers put away grief and trouble, trust the god and honour those who trust, fear lying and guard against backbiting, give up eating flesh and killing, give gifts and keep many austerities, not kill a kindness done or keep bad friends, never bear false witness or leave words of substance, keep near the assembly of the virtuous and avoid others, fear another's wife and protect suffering lives, guard the house of dharma and drive off what is not, and shun liquor, theft, lust, lies and idle company; since youth, wealth and body do not last, they should, without waiting on the days they have, seek the true companion for the land they will go to.
silappathikaram:30:186-202.nuance: After thirty kaathais of story the poem ends in plain commands, almost one to a half-line, and several of them name what the story has shown: false witness (the poor man seized by the spirit, 15:76-94), another's wife, flesh and killing. The list of things to shun (liquor, theft, lust, lies) resembles lay vows of the Jain and Buddhist traditions, but the unit names no school, so the claims are tagged general. The last three lines turn from conduct to impermanence: the reason for all the commands is the journey after death.

claims.claim: one should trust the god and honour those who trust
one should give up eating flesh and killing living beings
one should give gifts and keep austerities
one should not kill a kindness done, nor keep evil friends
one should never bear false witness
one should fear another's wife and protect lives in distress
liquor, theft, lust, lies and idle company are to be shunned
youth, wealth and the body do not last, so one must seek a companion for the world one goes to

links.note: Kovalan's midnight dream at Madurai has Kama casting his flower arrows on the bare ground and Madhavi giving Manimekalai before the dharma-one of the Bodhi; in the last kaathai Devanthi reports both as done, Kama flinging his bow and arrows on bare ground as Madhavi gives her daughter at the Bodhi.
links.teaches: The dream Kovalan feared as a sign of coming harm is fulfilled after his death in its other half, his daughter's renunciation, so the poem treats the dream as true in every part and lets the bad omen and the good one come out of a single night.

links.note: In the dream kaathai Saathan, having grown up as Maalathi's child and married Devanthi, shows her his ageless youth, tells her to come to his shrine and leaves, and she keeps worship there to win him back; in the last kaathai Maadalan retells this and the god returns by possessing her.
links.teaches: Devanthi's long worship to get her husband back is answered, but not as she asked: the god returns as a voice that takes over her body to reveal others' former births, so the husband she waited for comes back only as an oracle.

links.note: Maadalan once praised Kovalan as the compassionate hero who entered the rogue elephant's trunk to free an old Brahmin; in the last kaathai Maadalan says that this man, who entered the elephant's trunk to end the Brahmin's distress, has won the form of the gods.
links.teaches: The poem names one deed of Kovalan's, the elephant rescue and not his life with Madhavi or his wasting of wealth, as the deed whose fruit is his heavenly form, so the man the story often blames is judged at the end by his single act of risking his life for a stranger.

links.note: In the Manimekalai the materialist answers the question whether some have known a former birth by saying that the minds of those deluded by a god or by dreams are changed and such knowledge is mere doubt; in the last kaathai of the Silappathikaram former births are shown through a god possessing a woman and a sprinkled water, before a king's whole court.
links.teaches: The materialist's objection names exactly the means the Silappathikaram uses to prove former birth, a god's possession, so the sister epic records the reply a sceptic would make to this scene, and the scene offers as public proof what that sceptic rejects as the delusion of the possessed.

links.note: The patikam's third moral is that the deed of the past comes in wrath and makes one eat its fruit; the last kaathai states the law of births in full: the good reach the golden world, the loving go where their attachment leads, the fruits of virtue and wrong both ripen, and the born die and the dead are born.
links.teaches: The poem opens with karma as a vengeance that falls on Kovalan and closes with karma as an even law that also rewards and that lets love carry the mothers to rebirth beside the pathini, so the frame turns the threat of the opening into a consolation by the end.

links.note: The couplet says griefs that never let go hold those who hold attachment and do not let go; Maadalan says those whose hearts are full of love go where their attachment leads, and the mothers, held by love for Kannaki, are reborn near her temple.
links.teaches: The epic agrees with the couplet that attachment binds one to birth, but shows what the couplet does not: a bond of love that leads to a new birth beside the one loved, told without blame, so attachment's hold is the cost the mothers pay for staying near the pathini rather than only a grief.

gains.a: the epic's phrase பற்றுவழிச் சேறல் gains from the couplet the warning that the same hold is what keeps a soul from release, which Maadalan's calm statement does not say
gains.b: the couplet gains a case of attachment that is love for a virtuous woman and whose fruit, a rebirth near her, is told as a mercy, which tests its flat equation of holding with grief

links.note: Pattinathar's verse begins its list of the world's reversals with the born dying and the dead being born and turns from them to Siva, who frees from coming and going; Maadalan says the born die and the dead are born and calls it nothing new, the ancient way of life.
links.teaches: The same saying about the born and the dead serves the epic as a reassurance that the order of deeds holds and the Siddhar as a reason to loathe that order and seek Siva, so the line itself carries no verdict and its meaning depends on whether release or a good rebirth is the goal.

gains.a: the epic's law gains from Pattinathar the reminder that a round of births ordered by deeds is still a round, so the mothers' reunion is not release
gains.b: the Siddhar's formula gains a setting where it is said without disgust, as the Brahmin's comfort to a king, which shows that its horror in the Siddhar comes from his frame and not from the saying

links.note: The preface to the Patitruppattu's fifth decade says Senguttuvan, seeking a stone for the goddess-pathini, went through the forests, defeated the Aryan lord and bathed it in the Ganga; the last kaathai has the Chera endow the pathini's temple and the freed Aryan kings and Gajabahu of Lanka beg her to come to their lands.
links.teaches: The Sangam preface records the pathini stone as one deed among a king's conquests; the epic carries the story past the conquest, to the defeated kings themselves asking for the goddess, so the war for the stone becomes the way her worship spreads beyond the Chera land.

gains.a: the epic's scene gains from the preface an independent record that a Chera named Senguttuvan was remembered for fetching a pathini's stone from the north, though the preface itself is late
gains.b: the preface's single phrase about the pathini gains the cult that the epic says grew from it: a temple, a daily festival and a boon asked by foreign kings

links.note: The patikam opens with Ilango living at the eastern-gate shrine after giving up kingship; in the last kaathai the goddess tells why: when a man said he bore the mark of a future king, he looked at him in anger and put away the earth's burden to end Senguttuvan's distress.
links.teaches: The poet's renunciation, stated without cause in the first line of the poem, is explained only in its last unit and by the goddess herself, so the poem's frame makes the poet's giving up of a throne one more past act whose meaning the pathini reveals, like the former births of the mothers.

links.note: The Naladiyar quatrain, in its chapter on youth not lasting, says that since merciless Death roams looking for his people one should take provisions for the journey in good time; the epic's last lines say youth, wealth and body do not last and bid the hearers seek a true companion for the land they will go to.
links.teaches: The epic folds the Naladiyar's three opening themes, wealth, youth and body not lasting, into one line and draws the same conclusion of provision for the journey, but sets it after a list of concrete deeds, so the provision is named as truthfulness, not killing, giving and the rest rather than left as a figure.

gains.a: the epic's closing line gains from the quatrain the image of Death as a hunter who takes even the unborn, which is the urgency behind உளநாள் வரையாது
gains.b: the quatrain's undefined provisions (தோட்கோப்பு) gain a list of the deeds that make them up, given just before in the epic's commands

links.note: The couplet bids one do virtue without putting it off, because when one perishes it is the companion that does not perish; the epic bids its hearers not wait on their remaining days but seek the true companion for the land they will go to.
links.teaches: Read with the couplet, the epic's உறுதுணை is aram, the Kural's undying companion, and the epic adds that the companion must be sought before youth, wealth and body fail, after a story in which the dead carried only their deeds and loves into their next births.

gains.a: the epic's unnamed companion gains its identity from the couplet: it is virtue, not a person or a god
gains.b: the couplet's companion at the hour of perishing gains a destination, the land one goes to, which the epic has just shown as a new birth shaped by deeds and attachments

links.note: Maadalan told how a poor man who bore false witness against a chaste wife was caught in the noose of the devouring spirit, which would not take Kovalan's life in his place; among the poem's closing commands is never to bear false witness.
links.teaches: The command against false witness is the one rule in the final list that the poem had already shown punished on stage, by a spirit that refused even a willing substitute, so the bare imperative carries the weight of a remembered scene in which no one could pay another's penalty.

new_concepts.gloss: the chaste wife whose steadfastness gives her word power over kings, cities and nature
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word (பத்தினிக் கோட்டம், line 151)

new_concepts.gloss: the festival; a public feast of a god or a town
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word (நித்தல் விழாவணி, line 152)

source_issues: The kaathai has 202 lines in the core file, but the edition prints its last line as 200; the numbering here follows the core file.
Line 179: a stray space before a vowel sign was repaired in the core file (வாயிற்).
Line 164 reads றேழுந்த with a long ஏ, where the sense (a voice rose) needs எழுந்தது; probably a typing error for றெழுந்த.
Line 190 has a stray space before its semicolon (தாங்குமின் ;); the closing lines carry modern punctuation not found elsewhere in the kaathai.
Lines 97 to 111 run the cries of the three reborn girls together without naming who speaks which line; the division among them is inferred.
